Two genes average four RNA molecules per cell. One produces frequent small
bursts and the other produces rare large bursts. In this guide, you'll calculate
their RNA count distributions, compare the chance of observing zero molecules,
and separate old from new RNA after labeling.

> Run the examples in order. They use synthetic data and require only the installed package.

## Set up two bursting models

At steady state, mean RNA abundance is `km * B / d`. Here `km` is the burst
frequency, `B` is the mean number of molecules per burst, and `d` is the RNA
degradation rate. Use the same time unit for both rates and for labeling.

```{r libraries}
library(buRst)
```

Hold the degradation rate fixed at 1, and adjust burst frequency and burst size so that both models have an expected count of 4 RNA molecules:

```{r parameters}
models <- data.frame(
  model = c("Frequent, small bursts", "Rare, large bursts"),
  km = c(2, 0.5),
  B = c(2, 8),
  d = c(1, 1)
)
models$expected_mean <- with(models, km * B / d)
knitr::kable(models, digits = 2)
```

## Compare the count distributions

`burst_pmf_new()` returns possible counts (`k`) and their probabilities
(`prob`). Use `t_end = Inf` to obtain the steady-state distribution.

```{r compute-pmfs}
pmfs <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(models)), function(i) {
  burst_pmf_new(
    t_end = Inf,
    km = models$km[i],
    B = models$B[i],
    d = models$d[i],
    N = 64L,
    eps_tail = 1e-8
  )
})

# Check normalization on the computed support.
stopifnot(all(vapply(pmfs, function(x) abs(sum(x$prob) - 1) < 1e-6,
                     logical(1))))

moments <- data.frame(
  model = models$model,
  mean = vapply(pmfs, function(x) sum(x$k * x$prob), numeric(1)),
  variance = vapply(pmfs, function(x) {
    mu <- sum(x$k * x$prob)
    sum((x$k - mu)^2 * x$prob)
  }, numeric(1)),
  probability_of_zero = vapply(pmfs, function(x) x$prob[match(0, x$k)], numeric(1))
)
knitr::kable(moments, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Bursting model", "Mean", "Variance", "P(no RNA)"))
```

Compare the variance and the probability of zero RNA at the same mean. The
rare-large-burst model spreads probability across a wider range of counts.

```{r plot-pmfs, fig.cap="Predicted steady-state RNA count distributions for two models with the same mean."}
counts <- 0:25
p_small <- pmfs[[1]]$prob[match(counts, pmfs[[1]]$k)]
p_large <- pmfs[[2]]$prob[match(counts, pmfs[[2]]$k)]

plot(counts, p_small, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2,
     xlab = "RNA molecules per cell", ylab = "Probability",
     ylim = range(c(0, p_small, p_large)),
     col = "#08766E")
lines(counts, p_large, type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2,
      col = "#A74833")
legend("topright", legend = models$model,
       col = c("#08766E", "#A74833"), pch = c(16, 17),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

## Sample a small population

Draw 150 independent counts from each distribution. Compare the sample means,
variances, and fractions of zero counts with the probabilities above.

```{r sample, fig.cap="Illustrative synthetic cell counts sampled from the two predicted distributions."}
set.seed(2026)
n_cells <- 150L
samples <- lapply(pmfs, function(p) {
  sample(p$k, size = n_cells, replace = TRUE, prob = p$prob)
})

boxplot(samples, names = c("Frequent / small", "Rare / large"),
        ylab = "RNA molecules per cell", col = c("#B4D6E0", "#F5C6B8"),
        outline = FALSE)
stripchart(samples, method = "jitter", vertical = TRUE, add = TRUE,
           pch = 16, cex = 0.35, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("black", 0.35))
```

```{r sample-summary}
sample_summary <- data.frame(
  model = models$model,
  sampled_mean = vapply(samples, mean, numeric(1)),
  sampled_variance = vapply(samples, var, numeric(1)),
  sampled_zero_fraction = vapply(samples, function(x) mean(x == 0), numeric(1))
)
knitr::kable(sample_summary, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Bursting model", "Sample mean", "Variance", "Fraction with no RNA"))
```

## Follow old and new RNA during labeling

Start the first model in steady state and label new RNA for 1.5 hours without
changing its kinetics. **Old RNA** is the initial RNA that survives labeling.
**New RNA** is synthesized during labeling and survives until sampling.
**Total RNA** is the sum of the two pools.

```{r old-new-total}
p <- models[1, ]
label_time <- 1.5

new_rna <- burst_pmf_new(
  t_end = label_time, km = p$km, B = p$B, d = p$d,
  N = 64L, eps_tail = 1e-8
)
old_rna <- burst_pmf_old(
  t_end = label_time, d = p$d, steady = TRUE,
  km = p$km, B = p$B, N = 64L, eps_tail = 1e-8
)
total_rna <- burst_pmf_total(
  t_end = label_time, km = p$km, B = p$B, d = p$d,
  steady = TRUE, N = 64L, eps_tail = 1e-8
)

summary_pool <- function(df, label) {
  data.frame(pool = label, mean = sum(df$k * df$prob))
}
pool_means <- rbind(
  summary_pool(old_rna, "Old RNA"),
  summary_pool(new_rna, "New RNA"),
  summary_pool(total_rna, "Total RNA")
)
knitr::kable(pool_means, digits = 3)
```

The expected total abundance stays approximately constant because the system starts in steady state and the transcription and degradation parameters do not change. The *composition* changes: old RNA is degraded while new RNA is synthesized.

```{r plot-pools, fig.cap="Predicted old, new, and total RNA distributions after a labeling interval."}
plot_k <- 0:18
old_p <- old_rna$prob[match(plot_k, old_rna$k)]
new_p <- new_rna$prob[match(plot_k, new_rna$k)]
total_p <- total_rna$prob[match(plot_k, total_rna$k)]
plot(plot_k, old_p, type = "l", lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#A74833",
     xlab = "RNA molecules per cell", ylab = "Probability",
     ylim = range(c(0, old_p, new_p, total_p)))
lines(plot_k, new_p, lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = "#08766E")
lines(plot_k, total_p, lwd = 2, col = "#283B51")
legend("topright", c("Old", "New", "Total"),
       col = c("#A74833", "#08766E", "#283B51"),
       lwd = 2, lty = c(2, 3, 1), bty = "n")
```
